## Introduction

You may find it useful to use both a statistics book and one or two cognitive books in order to answer all the questions.

## The Study

A researcher decided to investigate mental imagery and, in particular, mental rotation of complex visual stimuli, following on from Cooper and Shepherd's (1973) research, which indicated that the extent of rotation required affected the time taken to perform a task.

Using a PC, a group of 10 participants were each presented with a series of 50 pairs of stimuli and asked to decide whether a target stimulus was the same as, or the mirror-reversed version of, a standard/comparison stimulus. Each of the standard/comparison stimuli were individually presented on the left hand side of the computer and consisted of a 2 dimensional representation of a complex 3 dimensional shape; each of the target stimuli, about which a judgement was required, were individually presented on the right side of the computer screen and rotated either 30 degrees from the vertical or 150 degrees from the vertical compared to the standard stimuli.

Each participant was instructed to decide as quickly as possible whether the target stimulus was the same as the standard stimulus, and indicate this by pressing the S key, or was the mirror-reversed version, and indicate this by pressing the R key. On 25 of the trials the correct answer was S, and on the other 25 trials the correct answer was R, but the order of presentation of trials was randomised. The computer recorded each participant's responses and at the end of the experiment calculated their mean response time in milliseconds for each angle. The participants were thanked and debriefed.

## Question 4: Statistical Test

**Choose and run an appropriate test to analyse the data (showing ALL calculations)**

### Acceptable Tests

Appropriate test is either:

- A **related t-test** by hand, OR
- A **Wilcoxon** by hand, OR
- A **paired samples t-test** conducted on JAMOVI etc.

::: {.callout-note}
Wilcoxon is technically the better option as not able to test parametric assumptions as part of this assignment.
:::

For the by hand calculations, students need to show **ALL THE STEPS** in the calculation, report the result, report the critical value, and explain the result (i.e., that it is significant).

### Expected Results

**Related t-test by hand:**

- t = 3.54
- Critical value = 2.262 for df = 9
- t must equal or exceed the critical value for significance at the .05 level, which it does
- Therefore result is **significant**

**Wilcoxon by hand:**

- T = 3
- Critical value = 8
- T must be equal to or less than the critical value, which it is
- Therefore **significant** at the .05 level

**SPSS/JAMOVI result:** t(9) = 3.54, p = .006

### Marking Breakdown

| Criteria | Scheme A | Scheme B |
|:---------|:--------:|:--------:|

| Choose right test but only show results | 5 | 6 |
| If said between and did all calculations for between | 0 | 0 |
| If calculations are wrong | -2 marks | -2 marks |
:::

## Question 6: Methodological Improvements

**Suggest two methodological improvements the researcher could make, if the experiment were to be repeated.**

Consider giving marks to any **TWO** sensible improvements to the methodology that are well justified.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Example Answers
- Increasing the sample size
- Choose from a specific population of interest
- Include more degrees of rotation
- Changing the IV in some way, e.g., choosing a different type of IV rather than a 2D computerised image
- Increasing/decreasing the number of trials
- Measuring accuracy as well as reaction time
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Marks
- Scheme A: **(10 marks – 5 each)**
- Scheme B: **(10 marks – 5 each)**
:::

## Question 7: Individual Differences in Mental Rotation

**If further research were to be conducted on mental rotation, do you think there would be any differences in performance, if:**

a) **The results of females and males were compared – why?**
b) **The results of journalists and architects were compared – why?**

*(One reason for each)*

### Marking Guidance

Award marks for an answer to both a) and b) which includes some explanation/reasoning, and possibly supporting research (but the latter is not an essential requirement).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Guidance for Part a) Males vs. Females

Fine if argue for gender differences as long as there is some explanation:

- Differences in visuo-spatial vs. verbal reasoning between the genders
- Differences in lateralisation (left brain/right brain activation)
- Research findings are mixed but there is some evidence that males are better than females at mental rotation tasks, but there is counter-evidence
- Could argue males will perform better
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Guidance for Part b) Architects vs. Journalists

Similarly, can make clear arguments that **architects may be better than journalists**. There is even some research to support this but not many will have found it.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Marks
- Scheme A: **(20 marks – 10 each)**
- Scheme B: **(15 marks – 7.5 each)**
:::

## Question 8: Ecological Validity

**Outline a more ecologically valid way in which mental imagery could be investigated** *(clue – e.g., involving travel plans, maybe)*

The more involved the proposal for a more ecologically valid experiment, the more marks you can award.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Ideas for Answers

- Suggesting tasks that do not involve presentation of computerised 2D stimuli
- Moving 3D shapes into a new configuration from memory
- Having to rotate 3D objects mentally before slotting them into the right space/hole
- **Travelling** – walking, driving, swimming, from one location to another / involving map learning - using maps or satnav that have been rotated, or they are not allowed to rotate / following verbal directions involving turns and rotations
- Walking, driving, or swimming through a grid or maze that has been committed to memory
:::

### Marking Guidance

Students could give a one-line answer to this, or a couple of sentences, but **increase the mark for those who give the most detail**, and in particular for those who outline the different aspects of the experimental design such as:

- State the hypothesis
- Give details of IV/levels (e.g., angles/spatial orientation/number of rotations involved/difficulty/directions)
- DV (time taken/number of errors, etc.)
- Procedure

::: {.callout-note}
I advised writing **half a page at least**.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Marks
- Scheme A: **(20 marks)**
- Scheme B: **(15 marks)**
:::
